question: to the Commission Sigrid Friis (Renew) Subject:

Google intends to require all application developers to register with the company, provide government-issued identification, pay a fee and accept Google’s terms and conditions for their software to remain installable on Android devices. Google further outlined an ‘advanced flow’ mechanism aimed at so-called ‘power users’, which would allow the installation of applications from unverified developers. However, this process involves a burdensome steps. Moreover, it is delivered through Google Play Services, meaning it can be modified, restricted or withdrawn by Google without requiring an operating system update or user consent. These developments raise concerns regarding compliance with the Digital Markets Act (DMA), which obliges gatekeepers to permit the use of third-party apps without imposing unfair, disproportionate or technically restrictive conditions. In the light of the above: 1.
Has the Commission been in contact with Google about these specific measures?
What actions is the Commission prepared to take to ensure that gatekeepers do not introduce de facto technical or procedural barriers that undermine the openness of platforms in the EU?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.6.2026) The Commission is aware of Google’s announcement to introduce a developer verification process starting from September 2026 in some jurisdictions (not including the EU based on publicly available information). The Commission understands that as a result of this process, Android will require that all applications (apps) are registered by verified developers in order to be installed on certified Android devices and that apps by unverified developers will be subject to a so-called advanced flow. The Commission is also aware of public campaigns such as ‘Keep Android Open’ which have emerged in reaction to Google’s announcement. Article 6(4) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA)1 obliges gatekeepers like Alphabet to allow and technically enable the effective distribution of apps on their operating system through third party app stores or the web. At the same time, the DMA also permits Google to introduce strictly necessary and proportionate measures to ensure that third-party software apps or app stores do not endanger the integrity of the hardware or operating system, provided that such measures are duly justified by Alphabet. The Commission is actively engaged in a regulatory dialogue with Alphabet – including in relation to these measures – and is diligentlyvmonitoring Alphabet's compliance with the relevant legal framework to ensure that apps, including open-source apps, can be effectively distributed on Android outside Google Play. The Commission is prepared to take appropriate enforcement action where necessary.
